title: Ukraine’s allies should make an offer to Russians before September’s ‘elections’
gist: Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries and logistics have, for the first time since 2022, made the war materially visible to ordinary Russians — fuel queues, blocked mobile internet, threatened e-commerce — just as Russia holds September 2026 Duma elections. Chatham House argues Ukraine's allies should bypass the Kremlin and publicly offer Russians a deal: if United Russia loses, Ukraine halts attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.

insights.claim: Russia's September 2026 parliamentary vote is structurally pre-determined: it runs over three days, no international observers are permitted, almost-unverifiable electronic voting is allowed in 33 regions, and all parties and candidates are vetted by the presidential administration.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat the headline result as noise; the tradeable signal is turnout, protest incidents and the size of the manipulation gap, not the seat count.
insights.quote: Electronic voting, which is almost unverifiable, is permitted in 33 regions.
insights.locator: The vote will extend over three days

insights.claim: Russians nickname their own parliament the 'crazy printer' for the speed with which it rubber-stamps whatever laws the Kremlin proposes, indicating the legislature carries no independent policy risk.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not price Duma composition as a policy variable for sanctions, mobilization or war financing; it is a legitimacy instrument, not a veto point.
insights.quote: a parliament that they have long nicknamed a ‘crazy printer’ – for the speed with which it rubber-stamps whatever laws the Kremlin proposes
insights.locator: This September, Russians will go to the polls

insights.claim: United Russia openly branded itself 'Putin's party' at its recent congress, converting the parliamentary vote into a direct referendum on Putin rather than on a party platform.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Any measurable protest vote transfers directly to Putin's personal legitimacy — a higher-stakes read than normal midterm party results.
insights.quote: United Russia, which at its recent congress openly called itself ‘ Putin’s party ’
insights.locator: But are ordinary citizens ready to register discontent

themes.theme: The war finally hits Russian daily life

insights.claim: For three years the Kremlin successfully insulated ordinary Russians from the war through rising wages, normal urban life and attractive army enlistment pay, but that insulation broke down in 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The domestic-cost regime in Russia has changed; models assuming indefinite home-front tolerance of the war need re-calibrating.
insights.quote: Wages were rising, affluent cities lived their ordinary lives, and volunteers joined the Russian army enticed by attractive wages.
insights.locator: Feeling the war

insights.claim: Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have produced nationwide gasoline scarcity, with queues at petrol stations stretching for hours.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Russian domestic fuel supply is now a live constraint — watch refinery outage rates, fuel export bans and crack spreads as the transmission channel.
insights.quote: Gasoline is becoming scarce across the country because of Ukraine’s attacks on refineries, with queues at petrol stations stretching for hours.
insights.locator: Gasoline is becoming scarce across the country

insights.claim: Ukrainian attacks on Russian warehouses have produced smoke visible from space and Russians are bracing for the collapse of the country's extensive e-commerce system.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Logistics and consumer-fulfilment infrastructure is now a targeted category — a new channel for Russian consumer inflation and retail disruption.
insights.quote: Smoke from burning warehouses is visible from space , with Russians bracing anxiously for the collapse of the country’s extensive e-commerce system.
insights.locator: Smoke from burning warehouses is visible from space

insights.claim: Russian authorities have blocked mobile internet and cellular communications 'for security reasons', stripping citizens of services they took for granted and adding a self-inflicted layer to wartime disruption.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: State-imposed connectivity blackouts are now a recurring cost to Russian consumers and digital businesses, and a leading indicator of regime security anxiety.
insights.quote: Authorities have blocked mobile internet and cellular communications ‘for security reasons’, depriving people of services they have taken for granted.
insights.locator: Authorities have blocked mobile internet

insights.claim: A rumoured imminent mobilization to support the war in Ukraine preoccupies many ordinary Russians more than the September election itself.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A post-election mobilization announcement is the key event risk to monitor; it would mark escalation and a second shock to Russian labour supply.
insights.locator: Indeed, many ordinary Russians will be more concerned

themes.theme: Russian public opinion: war-weary but passive

insights.claim: Around two thirds of Russians say peace with Ukraine is their greatest wish, and even German Gref — head of Russia's largest state-owned bank and a former economy minister — has said the same publicly.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Elite economic figures voicing pro-peace sentiment is a defection indicator; track state-bank and technocrat commentary as an early tell on negotiation appetite.
insights.quote: No wonder around two thirds of Russians call peace with Ukraine their greatest wish.
insights.locator: No wonder around two thirds of Russians

insights.claim: Casting a ballot in a closed booth is a far lower-risk form of dissent for average Russians than street protest or anti-regime social media posts, making elections the cheapest available channel for registering discontent under repression.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Under repression, ballot behaviour — not protest counts — is the better proxy for latent opposition; watch spoiled ballots and non-United-Russia vote shares.
insights.quote: Casting a ballot in a closed booth is certainly safer for average Russians than taking to the street or posting an anti-regime message on social media.
insights.locator: Casting a ballot in a closed booth

insights.claim: Despite war-weariness, Russians remain frightened, dispirited, and unwilling to admit that their own leaders bear responsibility for the war, so economic grievance is unlikely to convert automatically into political action.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Discount narratives that Russian economic pain mechanically produces regime pressure; the grievance-to-politics transmission is broken and needs an external trigger.
insights.quote: Russians are frightened, dispirited, and unwilling to admit that their leaders bear responsibility for the war.
insights.locator: Today this is far from obvious

insights.claim: The core proposal is that Ukraine's allies publicly promise Russians that if United Russia loses the September elections, they will ensure Ukraine terminates its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure — an explicit vote-for-relief bargain aimed at the population, not the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If Western capitals adopt any version of this, Russian refinery-strike tempo becomes an explicit political bargaining chip — directly relevant to crude and refined product risk premia.
insights.quote: if United Russia loses these elections, the allies will ensure that Ukraine terminates its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure
insights.locator: The offer

insights.claim: This conditional energy-strike offer is framed as more sophisticated than the blanket moratorium on long-range air attacks that Zelenskyy recently discussed with Trump, because it targets Russian voters rather than negotiating with Putin.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals that a US-brokered long-range strike moratorium is already on the table — a ceasefire-adjacent development worth tracking for energy and defence positioning.
insights.quote: This would be a more sophisticated offer than a moratorium on long-range air attacks, such as President Zelenskyy recently discussed with President Trump.
insights.locator: This would be a more sophisticated offer

insights.claim: Zelenskyy has since 2024 repeatedly proposed a reciprocal halt to strikes on energy infrastructure and Putin has refused many times, meaning the Kremlin — not Kyiv — is the blocker on energy-infrastructure de-escalation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect continued Russian refinery and Ukrainian grid attrition until Putin's cost calculus changes; a reciprocal energy truce is the single most bullish near-term de-escalation trigger.
insights.locator: Since 2024, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has been calling

insights.claim: A secondary benefit of the offer is that if Russians choose de-escalation and are not heard, the unheeded choice itself becomes an additional source of disillusionment with their government.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The proposal is designed as a no-lose information operation — a rejected offer still compounds regime legitimacy erosion over the medium term.
insights.locator: Second, it would be useful to communicate to Russians

insights.claim: At least 7–9 million people in Russia regularly access non-state media according to a recent CASE Centre study, and they relay what they learn to friends and relatives — enough of a channel to defeat the claim that any Western message is unreachable.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Quantifies the addressable audience for Western information operations in Russia — a small but non-trivial 7-9m base with second-order spread.
insights.quote: at least 7–9 million people in Russia access them regularly
insights.locator: True, Russia’s information sphere is tightly controlled

insights.claim: Populations under authoritarian rule display a keen sensitivity to when vote manipulation becomes too grotesque, as shown by Russia's 2011 protests and Belarus in 2020 — so falsified results carry their own destabilization risk.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Overt falsification is itself a tail risk for internal unrest; monitor the credibility gap between reported and expected results, not just the outcome.
insights.quote: people in authoritarian regimes tend to have a keen sensitivity to when vote manipulation goes too far or becomes too grotesque
insights.locator: Of course, in the Russian system the Kremlin will ensure

insights.claim: United Russia faction deputy leader Andrei Isayev publicly urged Russians not to react to refinery bombings like aggrieved 'teenagers', claiming Ukraine strikes refineries precisely to produce a Duma without a stable majority — evidence the Kremlin already fears an electoral backlash from war damage.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The regime's own messaging reveals its perceived vulnerability — Russian elite rhetoric about refinery strikes is a read on how much economic pain is politically biting.
insights.quote: So, if the enemy suspects and fears something, why not do what he’s afraid of?
insights.locator: Notably, Putin’s cronies already suspect

insights.claim: The counter-case is acknowledged in full — controlled media, Russian hostility to following Kyiv's lead, pre-determined results, and Kremlin exploitation of the move as proof of Western interference in Russia's 'domestic affairs'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The main downside is a Kremlin propaganda win on 'foreign interference' — a rally-round-the-flag risk that could harden rather than soften Russian positions.
insights.locator: Some would argue that this is a hopeless prospect

insights.claim: The author concedes the chance that such an initiative triggers change in Russia is negligible, but argues the expected cost is zero, making it a positive-expected-value asymmetric bet.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frame Western Russia policy as cheap-optionality bets rather than high-probability plays; low-cost information moves may proliferate ahead of the September vote.
insights.quote: What are the chances that such an initiative would trigger change in Russia? Negligible. But what would those behind it have to lose? Nothing.
insights.locator: What are the chances that such an initiative

insights.claim: Europe's decades-long posture of merely reacting to Russia while avoiding provocation of the Kremlin is judged a failure, and the recommendation is a shift to unconventional initiative.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A think-tank push toward more assertive, unconventional European Russia policy is an early signal of escalating European risk appetite worth watching in defence and sanctions policy.
insights.quote: The Europeans have spent decades merely reacting to Russia, doing their best not to provoke the Kremlin bear. The result can hardly be called a success.
insights.locator: The Europeans have spent decades merely reacting

insights.claim: The strategic addressee should shift from the Russian president and the Russian opposition to ordinary Russians, because any future 'new Russia' depends on that population rather than on exiled dissidents or elite negotiation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A doctrinal shift in Western Russia policy away from opposition-elite engagement toward mass-audience persuasion would reshape sanctions and information-policy design.
insights.quote: the time has come to address not the Russian president and not the Russian opposition, but ordinary Russians
insights.locator: This proposal is unconventional
